gui.jaymoskingdoms.astronomy_journal.ski: Fine enough to tell longitude bands apart (from rank %s).

Astrometry is measuring where things are on the sky. Each rank divides the step your readings are rounded to: 1° / (1 + rank). Finer readings open the longitude measurement, and the values written from then on are more exact.

Scholar is the fourth pillar of your skill tree (K). Its experience comes only from new measurements in this journal. Each level is a point, with a bonus point every fifth level, and its points are spent here, not on the web. A court wizard's unmaking or a bottle o' enchanting gives them back like any other pillar's. It adds nothing to your character level or attribute points, and earns no title.
gui.jaymoskingdoms.astronomy_journal.stu:
Astronomers draw the sky as a sphere with the observer at its centre. Every star has a fixed place on it, given by two angles.
Declination δ: degrees north (+) or south (−) of the celestial equator, from −90° to +90°.
Right ascension α: degrees east along the equator from a fixed zero point, 0° to 360°. Catalogues often give it in hours: 24 h = 360°, so 1 h = 15°.
Example: Vega is at α = 18.616 h × 15 = 279.23°, δ = +38.78°.
Where you see a star takes two other angles. Altitude: degrees above the horizon, 0° on it and 90° straight up. Bearing: degrees round from north through east, so east is 90°, south 180°, west 270°.
The stars are the HYG v4.1 catalogue: every star down to magnitude 6.5, 8,870 of them. A smaller magnitude is brighter. Sirius is −1.44; the faintest drawn are 6.5, about what an eye sees on a dark night.

The sidereal time S is the right ascension on your meridian now (the line from north, through overhead, to south). A star's hour angle H = S − α is how far west of the meridian it has turned.
With your latitude φ:
sin(alt) = sin δ · sin φ + cos δ · cos φ · cos H
bearing = 180° + atan2(sin H, cos H · sin φ − tan δ · cos φ)
Example: S = 241.07°, Vega α = 279.23°, δ = 38.78°, φ = 45°. Then H = −38.17° and sin(alt) = 0.6264 · 0.7071 + 0.7795 · 0.7071 · 0.7862 = 0.8763, so alt = 61.20°. The bearing comes to 88.9°: almost due east, and still rising, because H is negative.
A star stands highest on the meridian (H = 0), at alt = 90° − |φ − δ|. Vega reaches 83.8°; Sirius (δ = −16.72°) only 28.3°.
At φ = 45°, stars with δ above +45° never set, and stars with δ below −45° never rise.

A world day is 24,000 ticks (20 minutes). The time of day t starts at 0 at sunrise; 6,000 is noon and 18,000 is midnight.
The sky turns once a day, 360°, so 1° takes 66.7 ticks (3.3 seconds) and one tick is 0.015°.
The sidereal time at longitude λ on day d:
S = 360° · (t − 6,000) / 24,000 + λ + 0.9856° · d
Here d is the number of whole 24,000-tick days the world has run (the armillary shows Day d + 1). Sleeping through a night moves the clock, not d.
Example: d = 30, t = 20,000, standing 3,000 blocks east (λ = 1.5°): S = 210° + 1.5° + 29.57° = 241.07°, the S of the Vega example.
Where it parts from the real sky: the real sky turns once in a sidereal day of 23 h 56 m 4 s, a little faster than the Sun, and the 3 m 56 s gained each day builds the yearly drift smoothly. Here the sky turns exactly once a world day, and the drift is added as 0.9856° per day in one step, when d changes.

The sky turns about the celestial pole. From latitude φ the pole stands φ degrees above the north horizon, so the pole's altitude is your latitude.
Polaris (HIP 11767, δ = +89.26°) sits 0.74° from the pole, so its altitude swings between φ − 0.74° and φ + 0.74° as the sky turns. One reading of Polaris gives the latitude to within 0.74°, and the journal writes Polaris's altitude as it stood.
Example: here Polaris is seen anywhere from 44.26° to 45.74°, so a reading of 44.4° means a latitude between 43.7° and 45.1°. The true value is 45°.
The journal records the latitude once, the first time Polaris is among your discovered stars at a reading.
Where it parts from the real world: the latitude is 45° everywhere. Walking north or south changes nothing in the sky. On Earth 1° of latitude is about 111 km, and the pole would sink as you went south.

At one moment, an observer further east sees the sky further turned: their sidereal time is larger by their difference in longitude, Δλ = S₁ − S₂.
Every place here shares one exact clock, so a reading at a known t and d gives λ directly:
λ = S − 360° · (t − 6,000) / 24,000 − 0.9856° · d
Scale: 1° of longitude is 2,000 blocks east or west. North and south don't change it.
The journal counts one longitude for each band %s wide (%s blocks) you take a reading in. A reading can only tell bands apart if it is finer than a band, so this needs Astrometry rank %s, which rounds to %s.
Example: a sphere at x = 7,300 is at λ = 3.65°, in the band from 3.50° to 3.75°.
Where it parts from the real world: on Earth 1° of longitude is about 79 km at latitude 45°, and finding it this way needs a clock that keeps a distant place's time exactly. Here the clock is given.

Each day the stars stand 0.9856° further round at the same clock time, so each rises about 66 ticks earlier than the day before. After 360° / 0.9856° = 365.26 days the sky is back where it began: the sky's year.
Example: at midnight (t = 18,000) at λ = 0°, S = 180° + 0.9856° · d. Vega (α = 279.23°) is on the meridian at midnight when 0.9856° · d = 99.23°, so when d is about 101. Sirius (α = 101.29°) is, when d is about 285.
The journal cuts the sky's year into 12 months of 30.44 days and counts one reading in each, writing down how far the sky has drifted: 0.9856° · d, less whole turns.
Where it parts from the real world: the real drift comes from the Earth going round the Sun, so it also carries the Sun through the stars and makes the seasons. Here it is a rule of the stars alone. The Sun, the Moon and the world's seasons do not follow it.

No reading is exact. The journal writes each value rounded to the step the readings resolve: ε = 1° / (1 + rank of Astrometry).
Rank 0: 1°. Rank 1: 0.5°. Rank 4: 0.2°. Rank 9: 0.1°. Rank 20: 0.048°, or 2.9′ (1° = 60 arcminutes).
Example: Vega at an altitude of 61.197° is written 61° at rank 0, 61.2° at rank 4 and 61.19° at rank 20.
Only a measurement not yet in the journal counts: each star's place once, the latitude once, each longitude band once, each month of the sky's year once. Repeating a reading writes nothing and earns nothing, and a finer rank does not make an old measurement new.
Each new measurement is Scholar experience: a star's place %s, the latitude %s, a longitude band %s, a month %s. One reading writes at most %s new stars, the highest first, and the rings take %s seconds to settle before the next. Astrometry has %s ranks.
Where it parts from the real world: a real reading scatters around the truth by a different amount each time, and repeating it and averaging is how real astronomers beat the scatter. Here the value is exact, then rounded, so repeating it would only give the same number.

This sky is a model. These are the places it knowingly differs from the real one:
· The world is flat: the latitude is 45° everywhere, and the longitude is only how far east you stand.
· No refraction. Real air lifts a star near the horizon by about 0.5°, so real stars rise a little early. Here a star is up when its altitude is above 0°.
· No precession. The real pole circles once in about 26,000 years, about 1° every 72 years. Here the catalogue's places (epoch 2000) never change.
· No proper motion, parallax or aberration: the stars never move against each other.
· The Sun and Moon are the game's own. Its Sun passes straight overhead every day, which no Sun does at latitude 45°, and the star field is not tied to it: there is no ecliptic and no zodiac.
· On screen a star's brightness falls in a straight line with magnitude. Real brightness falls by a factor of 2.512 for each magnitude.
· Light pollution is a simple dimming near villagers, not a model of the sky's glow.
